questions.problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2})}$ is orthonormal
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is true. Indeed,

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}9 \\ 6\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}2 \\ -3\end{aligned}]=18-18=0.
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, $Q({u}_{1})⊥Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0.
$$

- Statement III is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})$ is not a unit vector since

$$
‖Q({u}_{1})‖=‖{u}_{1}‖=\sqrt{{9}^{2}+{6}^{2}}\ne 1.
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

questions.problem:
$$
{u}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}],\,{u}_{3}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 3 \\ -3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vectors above, and let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Which of the following statements are true?

- ${u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=0$
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})}$ is orthogonal
- ${Q({u}_{1}),Q({u}_{2}),Q({u}_{3})}$ is orthonormal
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

With that in mind, let's examine our statements.

- Statement I is false since

$$
{u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 3 \\ 5\end{aligned}]\cdot [\begin{aligned}1 \\ 4 \\ -1\end{aligned}]=2+12-5=9\ne 0.
$$

- Statement II is false. Notice that, for example, $Q({u}_{1})⊥̸Q({u}_{2})$ since

$$
Q({u}_{1})\cdot Q({u}_{2})={u}_{1}\cdot {u}_{2}\ne 0.
$$

- Statement III is false since the set is not even orthogonal.

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the statements are true."

questions.problem: Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Find $‖Q(x)‖$, where $x=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 3 \\ \sqrt{6}\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}‖Q(x)‖ & =‖x‖ \\  & =\sqrt{{x}_{1}^{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}+{x}_{3}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-1)^{2}+{3}^{2}+{(\sqrt{6})}^{2}} \\  & =4.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Let $Q$ be an orthogonal linear transformation. Find $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)$, where $x=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ and $y=[\begin{aligned}-7 \\ -5 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$
questions.worked_solution:
Since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have that $Q(x)\cdot Q(y)=x\cdot y$ for any vectors $x$ and $y.$

The linear transformation $Q$ being orthogonal is equivalent to the following:

- The matrix $Q$ of transformation $Q$ relative to any orthonormal basis (including the standard basis) of ${R}^{n}$ is orthogonal.

- $||Q(x)||=||x||.$

- If $x⊥y$ then $Q(x)⊥Q(y)$ for any $x,y\in {R}^{n}.$ In general, $Q$ preserves the angle between any two vectors.

- $Q$ maps any orthogonal (orthonormal) set into an orthogonal (orthonormal) set.

In this case, since $Q$ is orthogonal, we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(x)\cdot Q(y) & =x\cdot y \\  & =0\cdot (-7)+1\cdot (-5)+1\cdot 1 \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
